title: Euclidean Rellich compactness with a fixed compact support
statement: Over $\mathbf R$ [def-weil-field], let $m\geq1$ and $r\geq0$ be integers and let $K\subset\mathbf R^m$ be compact. Let $(f_n)_{n\geq1}$ be Lebesgue-measurable functions $\mathbf R^m\to\mathbf R^r$ modulo almost-everywhere equality, vanishing almost everywhere outside $K$. Assume that their first distributional derivatives belong to $L^2$ and $\sup_n(\|f_n\|_2^2+\sum_{j=1}^m\|\partial_j f_n\|_2^2)<\infty$, where $\|f\|_2^2=\int_{\mathbf R^m}|f|^2$ and $\langle\partial_j f,\varphi\rangle=-\int f\partial_j\varphi$ for compactly supported smooth test functions $\varphi$. There exist a strictly increasing sequence of indices $(n_k)$ and $f\in L^2(\mathbf R^m,\mathbf R^r)$, vanishing almost everywhere outside $K$, such that $\|f_{n_k}-f\|_2\to0$.

source.place: VI §2 Rellich lemma (2.2), printed p.289; supporting fixed-support Euclidean compactness. Supplemental online Demailly course Differential and pseudodifferential operators on manifolds, §2, Lemma 2.7 proof, pp.5–6 (t=1, s=0); its Euclidean derivative-norm form is stated here. WANTED locally; supplemental source read online at https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/analytic_geometry_2019/pseudodiff.pdf

proof.text: If $r=0$, every term is zero and the identity subsequence works. For $r>0$, choose $M>0$ bounding the displayed energy. Fix a coordinate $a$ and put $u_n=(f_n)_a$, viewed also as a complex function with zero imaginary part. Its scalar energy is at most $M$: the coordinate square is at most the vector norm square for the function and each derivative. The weak derivative identity passes to coordinates and to complex test functions by real and imaginary parts. We prove that $(u_n)$ has an L2 Cauchy subsequence; at the end we extract successively for the finitely many coordinates.

source.place: §2 Lemma 2.7, pp.5–6, t=1 and s=0; agent-written specialization and explicit details.

proof.text: Let $h_n(\xi)=\int e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}u_n(x)\,dx$. The fixed-support estimate gives continuous representatives with common bound $B=\operatorname{vol}(K)^{1/2}\sqrt M$ and Lipschitz constant $L=2\pi(\int_K|x|^2)^{1/2}\sqrt M$. The L1/L2 realization identifies these integrals with $\mathcal F_2u_n$ and gives $\|h_n-h_l\|_2=\|u_n-u_l\|_2$. Apply the existing weak-derivative Fourier identity with $\alpha=e_j$ and $v=\partial_j u_n$: its compact-test hypothesis is exactly ours, and all these functions are L2. Thus $\mathcal F_2(\partial_j u_n)=2\pi i\xi_j h_n$ almost everywhere. Taking squared L2 norms and using the realization's isometry gives $4\pi^2\int\xi_j^2|h_n|^2=\|\partial_j u_n\|_2^2$. Sum over $j$ and add $\int|h_n|^2=\|u_n\|_2^2$ to obtain $\int(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)|h_n|^2\leq M$.

source.place: §2 Lemma 2.7, pp.5–6, t=1 and s=0; agent-written specialization and explicit details.

proof.text: For each positive integer $j$, let $D_j=\{\xi:|\xi|\leq j\}$. The properness result over the usual locally compact field $\mathbf R$ makes $D_j$ compact, and over $\mathbf C$ makes the closed disk $Q=\{z:|z|\leq B\}$ compact. Restrict $h_n$ to $D_j$. These are bounded continuous maps with values in $Q$. The common Lipschitz constant gives equicontinuity directly: choose radius $\epsilon/(1+L)$ when $L$ is that constant. Ascoli therefore makes their closure compact in the uniform metric; the compact-metric subsequence theorem gives a subsequence converging in that metric on $D_j$. The same conclusion applies to any previously selected subsequence, since both bounds persist.

source.place: §2 Lemma 2.7, pp.5–6, t=1 and s=0; agent-written specialization and explicit details.

proof.text: Here is the simultaneous extraction. Start with the increasing index map $p_0(n)=n$. Recursively use the preceding compact-subsequence conclusion on $D_j$ to choose a strictly increasing $q_j$ such that $h_{p_{j-1}(q_j(n))}$ converges uniformly there, and set $p_j=p_{j-1}\circ q_j$. Define $n_k=p_k(k)$ for $k\geq1$. Since an increasing map on natural numbers has $q_{k+1}(k+1)\geq k+1$, we have $n_{k+1}\geq p_k(k+1)>p_k(k)=n_k$. For fixed $j$ and $k\geq j$, $p_k=p_j\circ t_{j,k}$ with $t_{j,k}$ a composition of increasing maps and $t_{j,k}(k)\geq k$. Thus the tail of $(h_{n_k}|_{D_j})$ samples the uniformly convergent sequence selected at stage $j$ at indices tending to infinity. It converges uniformly, and in particular is uniformly Cauchy, on $D_j$.

source.place: §2 Lemma 2.7, pp.5–6, t=1 and s=0; agent-written specialization and explicit details.

proof.text: Put $w(\xi)=1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2$. For two extracted terms and $R>0$, positivity and $|z-z^{\prime}|^2\leq2|z|^2+2|z^{\prime}|^2$ give $$\int_{|\xi|>R}|h_{n_k}-h_{n_l}|^2\leq\frac{4M}{1+4\pi^2R^2}.$$ Choose an integer $R\geq1$ making this less than $\epsilon^2/2$. On $D_R$, the same integral is at most $\operatorname{vol}(D_R)\sup_{D_R}|h_{n_k}-h_{n_l}|^2$. This is less than $\epsilon^2/2$ for sufficiently large $k,l$, since the volume of this bounded Euclidean ball is finite and step 4 gives uniform Cauchyness. Splitting the integral into the ball and its complement proves $\|h_{n_k}-h_{n_l}\|_2<\epsilon$. Plancherel then proves that $(u_{n_k})$ is L2 Cauchy.

source.place: §2 Lemma 2.7, pp.5–6, t=1 and s=0; agent-written specialization and explicit details.

proof.text: Apply the scalar construction first to coordinate 1, then to coordinate 2 along the chosen subsequence, and so on through coordinate $r$. Previously obtained Cauchyness persists under subsequences. The final index map is a finite composition of strictly increasing maps. The identity $\|f_{n_k}-f_{n_l}\|_2^2=\sum_{a=1}^r\|(f_{n_k})_a-(f_{n_l})_a\|_2^2$ shows vector L2 Cauchyness, by choosing the scalar errors less than $\epsilon/\sqrt r$. The Euclidean Sobolev graph result at $s=0$ says $W^{0,2}=L^2(\mathbf R^m,\mathbf R^r)$ is Hilbert, hence complete; let $f$ be this sequence's L2 limit. Finally $$\int_{\mathbf R^m\setminus K}|f|^2=\int_{\mathbf R^m\setminus K}|f-f_{n_k}|^2\leq\|f-f_{n_k}\|_2^2\longrightarrow0.$$ Thus $f=0$ almost everywhere off $K$, as required.

source.place: §2 Lemma 2.7, pp.5–6, t=1 and s=0; agent-written specialization and explicit details.
